answers.describe: Aurelius is the information layer AI relies on to make decisions. We maintain a live graph of the entities, relationships and events that form our world, connecting organizations, people, vessels, aircraft and every other entity to the events they're involved in, so organizations deploying AI have a digital twin of the world their models can act on. Customers access it through Console, our API platform: today they pull Aurelius data into their own models, and tomorrow they'll hand us the decision itself and get back a finished answer.
answers.mission: Our mission is to improve every decision an organization makes. Our thesis: the consensus is that defensible, high-margin cash flows in AI will come from the companies that control the models, compute, energy and training data. We believe the true long-term advantage is controlling the information models rely on when they make decisions. Every decision AI makes will depend on the company that controls that information.
answers.sauce: One graph that compounds. Every new use case, source or region we add makes every existing answer more complete, and every customer runs on the same graph. We built all four layers ourselves: collection (sensors, telemetry, access rights and our own hardware, built country by country and source by source), a backbone that moves sensitive information across borders securely and legally, models trained on our own data to resolve entities and link relationships, and Console. All four share one cost base, so more revenue means more data, better models and better products. Our team built the modern NSA's information systems and then rebuilt them at SOCOM. Very few organizations have ever had to collect and resolve information at global, petabyte scale; that experience took decades to build and doesn't exist elsewhere in the private sector. And everything we build deploys anywhere, including fully on-premise with all of our information and no external dependencies.
answers.like: The simplicity of the logo, although it's too simple in that it's not distinctive enough to be ours. The compression of the characters and the typeface. And the colors: we think they're very good and want to keep them as the base, though we're open to suggestions. Overall it's austere and precise.
answers.dislike: The logo is simple but not distinctive enough; there isn't enough there to make it ownable. We currently use Switzer, which isn't our long-term choice. We'd prefer Helvetica Now Display or something similarly standard, closer to Helvetica or to what Apple and SpaceX use. (Eventually we'd want our own custom typeface, but that's out of scope here.) We also struggle not to look like Palantir: many of the choices we make so a page reads as more than words on a page, like em-dash and // lockups and layered cards, come close to Palantir-esque. And the system was built for a slide deck, so it doesn't yet extend to a website or our product UI.
answers.look: Subtle palette, controlled and serious, quiet authority, own the infrastructure, engineered, not decorated
answers.feel: Trust, permanence, precision, discretion (a degree of secrecy), global infrastructure and backbone, preeminence, confidence without noise, and depth: the sense that we know our subject better than anyone.
answers.avoid: Anything ancient, Roman or mythological; we want the meaning of the name to come through in how we talk, not in how the brand looks. Anything that reads as a Palantir derivative. The bright, approachable SaaS-tool look (Middesk, Linear). The quirky, creative feel Anthropic has gone for. The neo-industrial / defense style (targeting overlays, spec-sheet callouts, bracketed program labels, technical-drawing layouts). And nothing militaristic or 'tacticool', surveillance-creepy, hype-driven or energetic.
answers.customer: Two customer types, each spanning both enterprise and government. Embedded: software companies that use Aurelius as the data backbone that makes their product and their AI perform better. They see us the way they see AWS, Azure or GCP, but for data rather than compute: data infrastructure that goes hand in hand with their compute infrastructure to make the whole product better. In the same way AWS lets any customer tap into "infinite" compute, we let customers tap into "infinite" data, without having to source and organize it themselves. Operational: enterprises and government organizations that use Aurelius in their own operations. Here we go beyond queries, bringing models on top of the graph to take on entire workflows: they hand us the decision and get back a finished answer.
answers.demographics: Senior decision-makers at organizations, not consumers: heads of product and data at software platforms; risk, compliance, onboarding and trade leaders at banks, insurers, lenders and logistics companies; and program and mission leaders in government and defense. Age, gender and location vary. What they share is responsibility for decisions that depend on information their own data doesn't hold, and they buy on proof.
answers.competitors: Most often, our real competitor is the customer building it themselves: convincing a KYC company not to source and organize this data on its own, or a government or bank not to build the capability internally, and to bring us in as a dependency instead. We haven't seen another company build this layer; most stop at the application layer. Around us are model labs, data platforms (Palantir, Databricks, Snowflake), application-layer companies (Altana, Persona) and training-data companies (Mercor, Micro1), and their success accelerates ours.
answers.competitorBrand: Not a competitor, but Palantir. They hit enterprise seriousness and a real cool factor at the same time: clearly technical, but sophisticated, and a company an enterprise can trust. They still play off the government look of being able to solve really hard problems.
answers.spaceBrands: Palantir, Scale AI, Anduril, SpaceX, and Cognition with Devin.
answers.inspoLike: Palantir and Scale AI are the most representative for us: both have worked hard on branding that feels enterprise-grade while still technically capable. Palantir has a simple, iconic mark that works everywhere; Scale AI moved from a very colorful identity to a black, white and beige one that's modern and timeless. Anduril and SpaceX can do so much with so little because their hardware looks incredible. Anduril can show its hardware and look cool, with a strong, restrained color scheme, and SpaceX gets by with a plain wordmark and monochrome imagery. Cognition and Devin show how a brand system can grow: Cognition's hexagons read as a brain, and Devin's mark splits out from them, so the product carries part of the company's identity. We'd love the same relationship between Aurelius and Console. Their styles are also widely copied, which is why we want our own lane.
answers.inspiredBy: Logos we admire: Palantir, which is iconic partly because it's a bit spooky; it's thin, hard and crisp, and simple but distinct enough that it doesn't look like everyone else. Neuralink, which did something unique that's still relevant today; we don't want ours to look like it, but its natural flow shows a thin icon can work. Oculus, which is too thick for us but very simple, and had the benefit of resembling the product. Figure, whose symbol is simple, unique and tied to its name; their typeface is too techno sci-fi for us, but the symbol is great. Cognition and Devin, where hexagons suggest a brain and the product mark splits out of the company mark. Scale AI, for being cool and modern while ending up in a really timeless place. More references are on our inspiration board; we'll follow up over email.
answers.logo: A simple, iconic mark is the key requirement, like Palantir's: thin, crisp, and simple but distinct. We want to lead with the symbol rather than the name, and be patient while the symbol alone comes to be recognized as Aurelius. It has to work on servers and infrastructure, on the website, and in software as a clickable app icon and favicon. We want to focus on circles and hexagons, with no triangles or squares. We'd love product marks, like Console now or Sphere later in hardware, to use parts of the company logo the way Devin's mark relates to Cognition's, but it isn't required and we don't want to sacrifice the main logo for it. We're not really interested in letter play on the A unless it looks incredible, and stacked marks feel overused unless they're clearly differentiated. We also don't want the mark to reference the Roman or classical meaning of the name.
answers.colour: A subtle palette that doesn't tell an energetic story: controlled and serious. We like the colors we use today (dark near-blacks, greys, white, and warm sand and stone tones) and want to keep them, with no pop color. Supporting colors are welcome when a specific piece calls for them, for example a blueprint-style blue background with white text for a diagram or product document, or a deep red or natural green, but they support that piece rather than define the brand. References for the feel: SpaceX, Palantir, Unreal Engine, Scale AI, Rivian and Arc'teryx.
answers.type: Clean sans serif. We currently use Switzer, but it isn't our long-term choice; we'd prefer Helvetica Now Display or something similarly standard, closer to Helvetica or to what Apple and SpaceX use, for its simplicity and sophistication. Spacing and width can do the expressive work: compressed or tightly tracked it can feel more technical, set more openly it feels calm. Eventually we'd want our own custom typeface, but that's out of scope for this sprint. We want to avoid styles that rely on extra symbols (brackets, slashes, arrows, plus signs) for emphasis.
answers.board: We'll follow up over email with Pinterest
answers.action: Request a briefing. For the next two years, we want a visitor to think: "I've heard a bit about you. I don't know exactly what you do, and your website is low-key, but based on what I've heard you can help us, and I'd like to learn more."
answers.messages: The website should be impression-based. We don't expect everyone who visits to understand what we do. The roughly thousand customers who need to will find us, and we'll find them, through other means. The site should leave an impression of seriousness and capability. 1. Why we do it. A bold statement of belief: every decision AI makes will depend on the information it can reach, and Aurelius is that layer. 2. The impact. Outcomes rather than explanations. The kind of statement we want to make, for example (illustrative): helping a global shipping company protect a fleet of 100 vessels, helping a major bank expand its operations into Latin America, or helping a ride-hailing company cut ride disruptions in Africa by 67%. 3. Depth. Visitors should leave with the sense that these people really know their subject, without needing to understand exactly how it works.
